etymology: Welsh; Williams, son of William, the surname distinguished by the name of his family farm, Pantycelyn (“the hollow of the holly”), by which the sweet singer of Wales is affectionately known.
biblical_def: William Williams of Pantycelyn (1717–1791), converted under the open-air preaching of Howell Harris, laid aside the physician’s calling to become the chief poet of the Welsh Methodist revival, that mighty outpouring by which the LORD stirred a slumbering nation to song. Denied ordination to a settled charge because of his revival preaching, he rode the length and breadth of Wales for near half a century, and out of that saddle-borne ministry poured some nine hundred hymns which taught a people to sing their theology. His masterwork, known to the English-speaking church as “Guide Me, O Thou Great Jehovah,” sets the pilgrim in the wilderness, dependent moment by moment upon the pillar of cloud and fire: “Bread of heaven, feed me till I want no more.” Here is no vague religiosity but the settled Reformed confidence of a soul kept by covenant faithfulness through “the barren land.” Williams sang the whole compass of redemption—the sovereign electing love of God, the sufficiency of Christ’s blood, the sure perseverance of the saints unto the “verge of Jordan” and the farther shore. He is honored as the hymnist through whom God gave Wales a singing faith, and his labours remind the church that sound doctrine set to melody lodges in the heart when sermons are forgotten.
webster_summary: The great Welsh hymnwriter of the Methodist revival, author of “Guide Me, O Thou Great Jehovah.”
webster_full: WILLIAM WILLIAMS PANTYCELYN, proper noun. Welsh poet and hymnwriter (1717–1791), styled “the sweet singer of Wales.”
A chief instrument, with Howell Harris and Daniel Rowland, of the Welsh Methodist revival under the sovereign hand of God.
Author of some nine hundred hymns in Welsh and English, teaching covenant theology to a whole nation through song.
Best known for “Guide Me, O Thou Great Jehovah,” a pilgrim hymn drawn from the wilderness wanderings of Israel.
A traveling preacher denied a settled parish, who made the saddle his study and the highways of Wales his pulpit.
scriptures: And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of a cloud, to lead them the way; and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light; to go by day and night:
But made his own people to go forth like sheep, and guided them in the wilderness like a flock.
And the LORD shall guide thee continually, and satisfy thy soul in drought, and make fat thy bones: and thou shalt be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters fail not.
Psa 40:3
And he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God: many shall see it, and fear, and shall trust in the LORD.
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle that sound theology belongs in the mouth of the singing church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry is preserved not to refute an error but to hold up an example. Williams of Pantycelyn is honored as a servant through whom God gave a whole people a singing faith, and the design of the entry is to fix in memory the marriage of doctrine and praise that marked the Welsh revival.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the church’s song is a means of grace and a vessel of truth, not mere sentiment. When the pilgrim sings “Guide me, O thou great Jehovah, pilgrim through this barren land,” he confesses at once his weakness and the covenant faithfulness of the God who leads His flock through the wilderness to Canaan. Let the modern church learn again to sing its theology rather than merely to feel.
roots_summary: The name binds a man to the farm of the holly and to the revival song of a nation.
roots_lines: Williams — the patronymic “son of William,” a common Welsh surname made singular by one man’s song.
Pantycelyn — the family farm, “the hollow of the holly,” by which the poet is lovingly named apart from all other Williamses.
The Welsh word emyn (hymn) took new life in his hands, wedding scriptural truth to native melody.
The wilderness imagery of Exodus supplies the frame of his greatest hymn, the redeemed as pilgrims led by cloud and fire.
The English rendering “Guide Me, O Thou Great Jehovah” carried Welsh revival theology into the hymnody of the whole church.
usage: “Williams Pantycelyn taught Wales to sing what the preachers proclaimed.”
“We sang ‘Guide Me, O Thou Great Jehovah’ and felt ourselves pilgrims in a barren land.”
“Nine hundred hymns from the saddle—such was the fruit of Pantycelyn’s wandering ministry.”

etymology: English form of the Greek Thomas (“twin”), joined to the Irish surname Kelly (from Ceallach, “bright-headed” or “contention”); the name of the Dublin hymnwriter who sang the exaltation of Christ.
biblical_def: Thomas Kelly (1769–1855), son of an Irish judge and himself trained for the bar, was brought under deep conviction of sin while preparing to defend the law, and finding no peace in the works of the law he was led by grace to rest wholly upon the finished work of Christ. Forsaking his prospects, he took orders, but his evangelical fervour so displeased the Archbishop of Dublin that he was silenced in the establishment; undaunted, he preached in unconsecrated halls and gave the remainder of his long life to the gospel and to sacred song. He composed some seven hundred and sixty-five hymns, of which the noblest exalts the ascended and glorified Redeemer: “The head that once was crowned with thorns is crowned with glory now.” Here Kelly sets the humiliation of Calvary against the coronation of the risen Lord, teaching the church to behold Him who bore the reed and the mocking robe now seated in majesty, “a royal diadem adorns the mighty Victor’s brow.” His hymns breathe the settled joy of a man who had exchanged his own righteousness for Christ’s, and who never wearied of that exchange through fourscore and six years. Generous to the poor of famine-struck Ireland, sound in doctrine, and steadfast in trial, Thomas Kelly is honored as a singer of the crown rights of the exalted Lamb.
webster_summary: Irish hymnwriter (1769–1855), author of “The Head That Once Was Crowned with Thorns.”
webster_full: THOMAS KELLY, proper noun. Irish evangelical minister and hymnwriter (1769–1855), born in County Queen’s (Laois).
Trained for the law, converted under conviction of sin, and turned to the ministry of the gospel.
Silenced within the established church for his evangelical preaching, he laboured in independent congregations.
Author of some seven hundred and sixty-five hymns exalting the person and finished work of Christ.
Chiefly remembered for “The Head That Once Was Crowned with Thorns,” a hymn of Christ’s exaltation.
scriptures: Php 2:9
Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name:
Heb 2:9
But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour; that he by the grace of God should taste death for every man.
His eyes were as a flame of fire, and on his head were many crowns; and he had a name written, that no man knew, but he himself.
And when they had platted a crown of thorns, they put it upon his head, and a reed in his right hand: and they bowed the knee before him, and mocked him, saying, Hail, King of the Jews!
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of the crown rights of the exalted Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry is preserved as an honored example, not as the correction of an error. Thomas Kelly’s memory serves to fix the eye of the church upon the ascended Lord and to commend a life laid down for the gospel after every earthly prospect was surrendered for Christ.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the exaltation of Christ as the settled ground of the believer’s joy. “The head that once was crowned with thorns is crowned with glory now”—the same Jesus who tasted death for His people now reigns, and the church that beholds His glory is armed against every fear. Let the singing saints look up from the manger and the cross to the throne.
roots_summary: The name of the exalted Christ’s singer, from “twin” and the bright Irish house of Kelly.
roots_lines: Thomas — from the Aramaic for “twin,” the apostle’s name borne by many a faithful man.
Kelly — from the Irish Ceallach, an ancient and honorable surname of Erin.
His conversion turned on the law’s inability to justify, driving him to the righteousness of Christ received by faith.
The thorn-crown and the glory-crown supply the great antithesis of his most enduring hymn.
The doctrine of Christ’s ascension and session at God’s right hand shapes the whole of his praise.
usage: “Kelly forsook the bar for the pulpit, and the pulpit for the hymnbook of the whole church.”
“We closed the service with ‘The head that once was crowned with thorns.’”
“His seven hundred hymns all circle back to the exalted Lamb.”

etymology: English; Henry (“home-ruler”), Francis (“free man,” or “the Frenchman”), and the surname Lyte; the name of the frail Devon curate who sang of light and evening.
biblical_def: Henry Francis Lyte (1793–1847), orphaned early and educated by charity in Ireland, gave his life to the humble seaside parish of Lower Brixham in Devon, ministering faithfully to fisherfolk while his own frame was wasted by consumption. His health failing utterly, he preached his last sermon and, watching the sun set over the harbour on an autumn evening, penned the hymn by which the church has since walked with him through the vale: “Abide with me; fast falls the eventide.” Every stanza leans upon the promise of Christ’s abiding presence: “I fear no foe, with Thee at hand to bless; ills have no weight, and tears no bitterness.” He died at Nice within weeks, his last recorded words “Peace! Joy!” From the same faithful pen came the great doxological hymn “Praise, My Soul, the King of Heaven,” a versification of Psalm 103 that summons the ransomed soul to bless the LORD who “pardons all thy transgressions.” Lyte laboured in obscurity, in weakness, and under the shadow of death, yet the LORD ordained that a dying man should give the whole church its evening prayer and its morning praise. He is honored as a pastor whose infirmity was made the vessel of a hymn that has comforted ten thousand deathbeds.
webster_summary: English pastor and hymnwriter (1793–1847), author of “Abide With Me” and “Praise, My Soul, the King of Heaven.”
webster_full: HENRY FRANCIS LYTE, proper noun. English clergyman, poet, and hymnwriter (1793–1847).
Orphaned young and schooled by charity; curate of Lower Brixham, a Devon fishing village, for many years.
Long afflicted with consumption, he laboured faithfully among the poor to the end of his strength.
Author of “Abide With Me,” written in the shadow of death, and “Praise, My Soul, the King of Heaven,” from Psalm 103.
Died at Nice in 1847; his hymns remain among the best-loved comforts of the dying and the mourning.
scriptures: But they constrained him, saying, Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent. And he went in to tarry with them.
Bless the LORD, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name.
Who forgiveth all thine iniquities; who healeth all thy diseases;
Heb 13:5
Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the comfort of Christ’s abiding presence unto death.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry is preserved to honor a dying pastor whose weakness the LORD made fruitful. There is no error here to correct, only an example of faithfulness in obscurity and affliction to hold before the church.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sufficiency of Christ’s presence in the hour of death. “Hold Thou Thy cross before my closing eyes; shine through the gloom, and point me to the skies”—such is the prayer of a man who leaned on the promise, “I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.” Let the church sing this hymn not as sentiment but as the confession of a faith that outlasts the eventide.
roots_summary: The name of a frail curate whose evening hymn became the church’s companion in death.
roots_lines: Henry — “home-ruler,” a Germanic royal name; Francis, “free man” or “Frenchman.”
Lyte — an old English surname, providentially near the word “light” that shines through his verse.
The Emmaus plea, “Abide with us: for it is toward evening,” supplies the very frame of his greatest hymn.
Psalm 103 furnishes the substance of “Praise, My Soul, the King of Heaven,” a doxology of pardon and redemption.
His long battle with consumption lends every line the weight of a man near the verge of Jordan.
usage: “Lyte wrote his evening hymn while the sun set over Brixham harbour.”
“They sang ‘Abide With Me’ at the graveside, and the tears had no bitterness.”
“From the same pen came ‘Praise, My Soul, the King of Heaven,’ his versified Psalm 103.”

etymology: English form of the Hebrew Jacob through Greek and Latin (James), joined to the Norman-French place-name surname Montgomery (“Gomeric’s hill”); the name of the Sheffield editor and hymnwriter.
biblical_def: James Montgomery (1771–1854), son of Moravian missionaries who died on the mission field of the West Indies, was reared among the Brethren and, though he wandered for a season, was recovered to a warm and steadfast evangelical faith. He became editor of a Sheffield newspaper and was twice imprisoned for the boldness of his convictions, yet he bore the reproach patiently and used his pen for righteousness. Of his some four hundred hymns, two stand as jewels of the church. “Angels from the Realms of Glory” gathers shepherds, sages, and saints to worship the incarnate Son—“come and worship, worship Christ, the newborn King”—setting the whole created order in adoration before the manger. “Hail to the Lord’s Anointed” is a majestic versification of Psalm 72, hymning the reign of the promised King whose “kingdom still increasing, a kingdom without end,” shall break oppression, bless the poor, and stretch from sea to sea. Montgomery also gave the church its finest hymn on prayer, “Prayer is the soul’s sincere desire.” A layman singing amid the world’s traffic, twice jailed yet unbroken, he is honored as a hymnist who wedded the loftiness of the Psalms to the sure hope of Christ’s advancing kingdom.
webster_summary: English editor and hymnwriter (1771–1854), author of “Angels from the Realms of Glory” and “Hail to the Lord’s Anointed.”
webster_full: JAMES MONTGOMERY, proper noun. Scottish-born English poet, newspaper editor, and hymnwriter (1771–1854).
Son of Moravian missionaries who died abroad in the West Indies; reared among the Brethren.
Editor at Sheffield, twice imprisoned for his outspoken convictions, yet unbroken in faith.
Author of some four hundred hymns, including a beloved versification of Psalm 72.
Chiefly remembered for “Angels from the Realms of Glory,” “Hail to the Lord’s Anointed,” and “Prayer Is the Soul’s Sincere Desire.”
scriptures: Psa 72:8
He shall have dominion also from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth.
Yea, all kings shall fall down before him: all nations shall serve him.
Luk 2:13
And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God, and saying,
Isa 61:1

The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound;
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the hope of Messiah’s advancing kingdom.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry is preserved to honor a layman who used the editor’s desk and the poet’s pen for the kingdom of Christ, and who bore imprisonment for conscience without bitterness. It is an example, not a doctrine to be defended against distortion.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reign of Christ, the Lord’s Anointed, whose kingdom truly advances in the earth. “He comes with succour speedy to those who suffer wrong; to help the poor and needy, and bid the weak be strong.” Let the church sing Psalm 72 with confidence that the Son shall have dominion from sea to sea, and let this hope stir her to worship and to mission.
roots_summary: The name of a jailed editor who sang the manger and the throne of the Anointed King.
roots_lines: James — the English form of Jacob, “supplanter,” borne by apostles and kings alike.
Montgomery — a Norman place-name surname, “Gomeric’s hill,” carried into Britain by conquest.
The Moravian missionary heritage of his parents stamped his verse with a global, gospel-spreading vision.
Psalm 72 supplies the royal frame of “Hail to the Lord’s Anointed,” a hymn of Messiah’s reign.
The angelic host of Luke 2 opens “Angels from the Realms of Glory,” summoning all to worship the newborn King.
usage: “Montgomery was twice in prison, yet his hymns crown Christ as King.”
“At Advent we sing ‘Angels from the Realms of Glory’ and call all creation to worship.”
“‘Hail to the Lord’s Anointed’ is Psalm 72 made a coronation song.”

etymology: English; Frances (feminine of Francis, “free”), the middle name Ridley given in honor of the martyr Bishop Nicholas Ridley, and the surname Havergal; the name of the “consecration” hymnwriter.
biblical_def: Frances Ridley Havergal (1836–1879), daughter of an English clergyman and hymn-tune composer, was a woman of rare piety, learning, and delicacy of health, who could recite the whole of the New Testament, the Psalms, Isaiah, and the Minor Prophets from memory. Converted at fourteen and thereafter wholly given to Christ, she poured her short life into hymns and devotional writings that press upon the believer the surrender of every faculty to the Lord who bought her. Her best-loved hymn, “Take My Life, and Let It Be,” written after a night in which the LORD gave her the joy of leading a whole houseful of guests to peace, offers the members of the body one by one upon the altar: “Take my hands, and let them move at the impulse of Thy love; take my feet, and let them be swift and beautiful for Thee.” It is a hymn of thoroughgoing consecration flowing not from law but from the constraining love of Christ. So earnest was she in the surrender of the silver and gold stanza that she gathered up her own jewellery and sent it to the mission cause. Frail in body but resolute in soul, she is honored as a singer of entire devotion, whose watchword—“ever, only, all for Thee”—still calls the church to lay her all before the Redeemer.
webster_summary: English hymnwriter (1836–1879), author of “Take My Life, and Let It Be.”
webster_full: FRANCES RIDLEY HAVERGAL, proper noun. English poet, hymnwriter, and devotional author (1836–1879).
Daughter of clergyman and composer William Henry Havergal; named Ridley for the Reformation martyr.
A woman of deep piety and memory, able to recite large portions of Scripture by heart.
Author of “Take My Life, and Let It Be” and many hymns of consecration and trust.
Frail in health, she died at forty-two, having given her whole self to the service of Christ.
scriptures: Rom 12:1
I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.
For the love of Christ constraineth us; because we thus judge, that if one died for all, then were all dead:
For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God’s.
Gal 2:20

I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me.
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; her life recovers the principle of entire consecration to Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry is preserved to honor a godly woman whose whole life illustrated the surrender her hymns commend. There is no error to refute, only a bright example of devotion to set before the church.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the entire consecration of the believer, springing not from bondage but from the constraining love of Christ. “Take my life, and let it be consecrated, Lord, to Thee”—such surrender is the reasonable service of those bought with a price. Let the singing church learn from Havergal that holiness is the glad offering of a redeemed and grateful heart.
roots_summary: The name of a consecrated singer, marked by the memory of a Reformation martyr.
roots_lines: Frances — the feminine of Francis, “free” or “the Frenchman.”
Ridley — given in honor of Nicholas Ridley, burned at Oxford in 1555 for the gospel.
Havergal — her father’s surname, a house given to sacred music and psalmody.
Romans 12:1 supplies the theme of her life and hymns—the body presented a living sacrifice.
“Ever, only, all for Thee” became the watchword of her consecration and her verse.
usage: “Havergal sent her jewels to the mission fund, so wholly did she mean ‘take my silver and my gold.’”
“We sang ‘Take My Life, and Let It Be’ and offered ourselves anew.”
“Her watchword was ‘ever, only, all for Thee.’”

etymology: English; Catherine (from the Greek, traditionally rendered “pure”), joined to the surname Winkworth; the name of the great translator who gave the English church the treasures of German hymnody.
biblical_def: Catherine Winkworth (1827–1878), an Englishwoman of Manchester and Bristol, is honored not chiefly as an original poet but as the foremost translator through whom the rich hymnody of the German Reformation and the Lutheran centuries was borne into the English tongue. In her Lyra Germanica and later Chorale Book for England she rendered hundreds of German hymns with such fidelity and grace that they became the settled possession of English-speaking Christians, who often know them not as translations at all. By her hand the church received Rinkart’s great thanksgiving, “Now Thank We All Our God, with heart and hands and voices,” a hymn wrung out of the sufferings of the Thirty Years’ War yet overflowing with gratitude to “the God whom earth and heaven adore.” Through her too came Neander’s “Praise to the Lord, the Almighty” and Luther-era chorales that carry the doctrine of grace in every stanza. She laboured also for the education of women, but her enduring monument is this ministry of translation, a quiet and self-effacing labour that enriched the praise of millions. Catherine Winkworth is honored as a handmaid of the church’s song, who counted it a high calling to make the praises of one age and tongue the inheritance of another, that with heart and hands and voices the whole church might thank her God.
webster_summary: English translator (1827–1878) who rendered the great German hymns into English, including “Now Thank We All Our God.”
webster_full: CATHERINE WINKWORTH, proper noun. English translator of German hymnody (1827–1878).
Author of Lyra Germanica and the Chorale Book for England, standard collections of translated hymns.
The chief means by which Reformation-era and Lutheran German hymns entered English worship.
Translator of “Now Thank We All Our God,” “Praise to the Lord, the Almighty,” and many chorales.
Also an advocate for women’s education, yet remembered above all for her hymn translations.
scriptures: Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise: be thankful unto him, and bless his name.
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you.
Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits:
corruption_summary: A faithful labourer, not a contested doctrine; her work recovers the principle of thankful, doctrine-laden congregational song.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry is preserved to honor a quiet and fruitful labour—the translation of the church’s song across the barrier of tongues—which enriched English worship beyond measure. There is no error to correct, only a self-effacing example to commend.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the church’s call to thankful praise grounded in sound doctrine. “Now thank we all our God, with heart and hands and voices, who wondrous things hath done”—a hymn born in war yet brimming with gratitude teaches the church to give thanks in every thing. Let the church value her translators as she values her poets, for both serve the singing of the word of Christ dwelling richly in the saints.
roots_summary: The name of the translator who made the German chorales the inheritance of the English church.
roots_lines: Catherine — from the Greek, traditionally understood as “pure,” a name of ancient Christian honor.
Winkworth — an English surname borne by a family of piety and learning.
Lyra Germanica — her collection whose title means “the German lyre,” the harp of German praise.
The Thirty Years’ War is the crucible of Rinkart’s “Now Thank We All Our God,” which she Englished.
The Reformation heritage of Luther, Neander, and Rinkart passed through her pen into English worship.
usage: “Winkworth gave us ‘Now Thank We All Our God’ without our knowing it was German.”
“Her Lyra Germanica carried the chorales of the Reformation into English hands.”
“The translator’s labour is a ministry to the church’s song no less than the poet’s.”

etymology: English; Ray, a short form of Raymond (“wise protector”), joined to the surname Palmer (a pilgrim who had borne a palm from the Holy Land); the name of the American Congregational hymnwriter.
biblical_def: Ray Palmer (1808–1887), a New England Congregational minister, is remembered above all for a single hymn written in the fervour of his youth. As a young man of two-and-twenty, weary, ill, and far from home, he penned in his private notebook a poem born out of his own soul’s casting itself wholly upon the Saviour, never intending it for public use: “My faith looks up to Thee, Thou Lamb of Calvary, Saviour divine.” The verses came, he said, with such feeling that he could scarcely write them for weeping. Two years later Lowell Mason, meeting him in the street of Boston and asking for something to set to music, received this poem, and having read it declared, “You may live many years and do many things, but I think you will be best known to posterity as the author of ‘My Faith Looks Up to Thee.’” So it proved. The hymn is a jewel of evangelical faith, casting the sinner upon the Lamb, praying that grace would “take all my guilt away,” and looking to the pilgrim’s end when the “stream of death” is safely past. A faithful pastor of long and useful ministry, Ray Palmer is honored as the singer of a simple, personal, wholehearted trust in Christ crucified.
webster_summary: American Congregational minister and hymnwriter (1808–1887), author of “My Faith Looks Up to Thee.”
webster_full: RAY PALMER, proper noun. American Congregational clergyman and hymnwriter (1808–1887).
Born in Little Compton, Rhode Island; educated at Yale; long a faithful pastor in New England.
Author of “My Faith Looks Up to Thee,” written in his youth as a private expression of trust.
The hymn was set to music by Lowell Mason, who foretold it would be his most enduring work.
Wrote and translated other hymns, but is remembered chiefly for this one song of faith in the Lamb.
scriptures: Joh 1:29
The next day John seeth Jesus coming unto him, and saith, Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.
Heb 12:2
Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.
Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else.
But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot:
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of simple, personal faith in the Lamb.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry is preserved to honor a hymn born in private devotion and given by providence to the whole church. There is no error to refute, only a pattern of heartfelt trust to set before the believer.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the looking of faith away from self to Christ alone. “My faith looks up to Thee, Thou Lamb of Calvary”—this is the essence of saving faith, the eye of the soul fixed on the Lamb who takes away sin. Let the church sing it as the confession of a trust that neither begins nor ends in the self, but rests wholly upon the crucified Saviour.
roots_summary: The name of a pastor whose youthful prayer became the church’s hymn of trust.
roots_lines: Ray — a short form of Raymond, “wise protector” or “counsel-protection.”
Palmer — originally a pilgrim who bore a palm branch from the Holy Land, a fitting name for a hymnist.
The title “Lamb of God” from John 1:29 stands at the head of his greatest hymn.
Lowell Mason, the father of American hymn-tunes, gave the words their enduring melody, Olivet.
The looking of faith—“looking unto Jesus”—is the animating theme of the whole hymn.
usage: “Palmer wrote ‘My Faith Looks Up to Thee’ for himself, never meaning it for the church.”
“Lowell Mason foretold he would be best known for that one hymn, and so he is.”
“We sang it and looked away from ourselves to the Lamb of Calvary.”

etymology: English; John (from the Hebrew, “the LORD is gracious”), joined to the Yorkshire surname Fawcett; the name of the Baptist pastor who sang the communion of saints.
biblical_def: John Fawcett (1740–1817), converted in his youth under the preaching of George Whitefield, became a Baptist pastor at Wainsgate and later Hebden Bridge in Yorkshire, where he laboured faithfully among a poor and loving people for the whole of a long ministry. The story most treasured of him is that, called to a large and prosperous church in London, he had his goods loaded upon the wagons to depart, until the tears and entreaties of his flock so moved him and his wife that they unloaded the wagons and resolved to stay among the humble people who loved them. Out of that parting-that-was-not came his best-loved hymn, “Blest be the tie that binds our hearts in Christian love; the fellowship of kindred minds is like to that above.” It is the church’s hymn of communion, sung at partings and at the Lord’s table, tracing the “fellowship of kindred minds” to its source in the shared throne of grace: “before our Father’s throne we pour our ardent prayers.” A learned man who declined a doctorate and a wider stage to remain a shepherd of the lowly, Fawcett is honored as the singer of the communion of saints, that sweet fellowship which is the foretaste of heaven.
webster_summary: English Baptist pastor and hymnwriter (1740–1817), author of “Blest Be the Tie That Binds.”
webster_full: JOHN FAWCETT, proper noun. English Baptist minister and hymnwriter (1740–1817).
Converted under George Whitefield; long the beloved pastor of a humble Yorkshire congregation.
Famously declined a larger London charge to remain with the people who loved him.
Author of “Blest Be the Tie That Binds,” the church’s hymn of Christian fellowship.
A learned and useful pastor who prized the shepherd’s work above position or renown.
scriptures: Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles’ doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.
Col 3:14
And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness.
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of the communion of saints.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry is preserved to honor a pastor who chose the love of a lowly flock over the honor of a great pulpit, and who gave the church its dearest hymn of fellowship. There is no error to refute, only a shepherd’s faithfulness to commend.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the communion of saints, that fellowship of kindred minds bound together in Christian love. “Blest be the tie that binds our hearts in Christian love”—this tie is no mere sentiment but the fruit of shared prayer, shared burdens, and the one blood that cleanses all. Let the church sing it and cherish the fellowship that is a foretaste of the fellowship above.
roots_summary: The name of a Baptist shepherd who sang the sweet bond of Christian fellowship.
roots_lines: John — “the LORD is gracious,” the beloved apostle’s name and a staple of Christian households.
Fawcett — a Yorkshire surname, rooted in the northern dales where he ministered.
The “unloaded wagons” of Wainsgate frame the story behind “Blest Be the Tie That Binds.”
Psalm 133 supplies the theme—the goodness and pleasantness of brethren dwelling in unity.
The communion of saints, confessed in the creeds, is the doctrine his hymn sets to melody.
usage: “Fawcett unloaded the wagons and stayed with the people who wept to keep him.”
“We joined hands and sang ‘Blest Be the Tie That Binds.’”
“His hymn makes the parting of saints a foretaste of the reunion above.”

etymology: English; Robert (Germanic, “bright fame”), joined to the patronymic surname Robinson (“son of Robin,” itself a diminutive of Robert); the name of the hymnwriter who sang of grace and of the prone heart.
biblical_def: Robert Robinson (1735–1790), converted in his youth under the preaching of George Whitefield after a wayward and troubled early life, became a Baptist minister at Cambridge and a man of considerable gifts. In the flush of his early faith, at about the age of two-and-twenty, he wrote the hymn by which the whole church knows him: “Come, Thou Fount of every blessing, tune my heart to sing Thy grace.” It is a hymn of the streams of mercy, of the Ebenezer stone of help, and—most piercingly—of the honest confession of a heart still prone to wander: “Prone to wander, Lord, I feel it, prone to leave the God I love; here’s my heart, O take and seal it, seal it for Thy courts above.” Robinson knew his own frame, and in later years his own steadfastness was tried; yet the hymn stands as one of the most searching confessions of the believer’s need of sovereign, keeping grace ever penned. It teaches the church that even the saved heart must be tuned by grace, bound by grace, and sealed by grace unto the day of redemption. Robert Robinson is honored as the singer who set forth both the fountain of free grace and the sinner’s ceaseless dependence upon it.
webster_summary: English hymnwriter (1735–1790), author of “Come, Thou Fount of Every Blessing.”
webster_full: ROBERT ROBINSON, proper noun. English Baptist minister and hymnwriter (1735–1790).
Converted in youth under George Whitefield after a wayward beginning; long a preacher at Cambridge.
Author of “Come, Thou Fount of Every Blessing,” written in the early years of his faith.
The hymn confesses both the free grace of God and the heart’s proneness to wander from Him.
A gifted man whose own steadfastness was tried, yet whose hymn ministers keeping grace to millions.
scriptures: Then Samuel took a stone, and set it between Mizpeh and Shen, and called the name of it Ebenezer, saying, Hitherto hath the LORD helped us.
Jer 2:13
For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
Eph 4:30
And grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption.
Php 1:6
Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his hymn recovers the principle of sovereign keeping grace over a wandering heart.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry is preserved to honor a hymn of rare honesty—one that names the believer’s own proneness to wander and casts him upon sovereign grace to keep him. There is no error to correct, but a searching confession to lay upon the church’s heart.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the keeping, sealing grace of God over hearts still prone to stray. “Prone to wander, Lord, I feel it, prone to leave the God I love; here’s my heart, O take and seal it”—this is no license to sin but a cry for the grace that alone preserves the saints unto glory. Let the church sing it soberly, confident that He who began the good work will perform it unto the day of Christ.
roots_summary: The name of the singer of free grace and the heart’s need to be kept.
roots_lines: Robert — “bright fame” from the Germanic, a name of Norman kings and English commoners alike.
Robinson — “son of Robin,” a diminutive of Robert, one of the commonest English surnames.
The “Ebenezer” of 1 Samuel 7:12—“hitherto hath the LORD helped us”—stands in the second stanza.
The “fount of living waters” and the “streams of mercy” draw upon the fountain imagery of Scripture.
The sealing of the Spirit unto the day of redemption grounds the closing plea of the hymn.
usage: “Robinson wrote ‘Come, Thou Fount’ while yet a young man in the first fervour of grace.”
“We raised our Ebenezer and sang, ‘hitherto Thy help I’ve come.’”
“No hymn confesses the prone heart more plainly, nor pleads keeping grace more earnestly.”

etymology: Hebrew Elisheba (“God is an oath” or “God is my fullness”) through the Greek Elizabeth, joined to the Scottish surname Clephane; the name of the frail Scottish poetess of the cross.
biblical_def: Elizabeth Cecilia Clephane (1830–1869), a Scotswoman of Melrose in the Borders, was a frail and quiet soul, tender to the poor and afflicted, who gave away nearly all she had to the needy and was called by the villagers “the Sunbeam.” She died at only nine-and-thirty, and most of her hymns were published after her death; yet through her brief life the LORD gave the church two enduring songs. “Beneath the Cross of Jesus” sets the believer in the shadow of “a mighty Rock within a weary land,” content to lose all boast but one: “my glory all the cross.” It is a hymn of penitent adoration before the crucified Lord, tracing every stanza back to Calvary. Her other great hymn, “The Ninety and Nine,” sings the parable of the shepherd who leaves the flock to seek the one lost sheep upon the mountains cold, and who bears it home rejoicing though His own were “shed for one who had gone astray.” Popularized by the singer Ira Sankey in the Moody campaigns, it carried the seeking love of Christ to multitudes. Frail in body, brief in years, and hidden in a Border village, Elizabeth Clephane is honored as a singer of the cross and of the Shepherd’s seeking love.
webster_summary: Scottish hymnwriter (1830–1869), author of “Beneath the Cross of Jesus” and “The Ninety and Nine.”
webster_full: ELIZABETH CLEPHANE, proper noun. Scottish poet and hymnwriter (1830–1869) of Melrose in the Borders.
A frail and generous soul, called “the Sunbeam” for her kindness to the poor and afflicted.
Died at thirty-nine; most of her hymns were published after her death.
Author of “Beneath the Cross of Jesus,” a hymn of adoration before the crucified Lord.
Author of “The Ninety and Nine,” made famous by Ira Sankey in the Moody evangelistic campaigns.
scriptures: Luk 15:4
What man of you, having an hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it?
Gal 6:14
But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world.
Isa 32:2
And a man shall be as an hiding place from the wind, and a covert from the tempest; as rivers of water in a dry place, as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land.
I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; her hymns recover the glory of the cross and the seeking love of the Shepherd.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry is preserved to honor a frail and generous woman whose brief, hidden life the LORD made fruitful in song. There is no error to refute, only an example of quiet devotion and a cross-centered praise to commend.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the glory of the cross and the sovereign, seeking love of the Good Shepherd. “I take, O cross, thy shadow for my abiding place; I ask no other sunshine than the sunshine of His face”—such is the settled boast of one who glories in nothing save the cross. Let the church sing of the Shepherd who leaves the ninety and nine to bear the lost one home rejoicing.
roots_summary: The name of a Border poetess whose two hymns exalt the cross and the seeking Shepherd.
roots_lines: Elizabeth — from the Hebrew Elisheba, “God is an oath,” the name of Zacharias’ wife.
Clephane — an old Scottish surname of the Border country where she lived and died.
The parable of Luke 15 supplies the very substance of “The Ninety and Nine.”
Galatians 6:14—“God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross”—is the heart of “Beneath the Cross of Jesus.”
Ira Sankey’s impromptu setting carried “The Ninety and Nine” through the Moody campaigns to multitudes.
usage: “Melrose called her ‘the Sunbeam’ for her kindness to the poor.”
“We sang ‘Beneath the Cross of Jesus’ and took the cross’s shadow for our abiding place.”
“Sankey’s singing of ‘The Ninety and Nine’ moved thousands to the Shepherd who sought them.”
